To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the honeybee uses different behavioral prototypes during homing, depending on its distance to the goal and the visual cues surrounding it.

1) the honeybee’s flight behavior can be decomposed into a small number of prototypical movements that reflect the bees’ saccadic pattern; 2) the occurrence of these prototypical movements depends on the bees' distance to the landmark and the feeder; 3) the occurrence of specific prototypical movements depends also on the visual appearance of the landmarks.

the honeybees’ homing flight behavior is composed of a set of prototypical components that can be used to identify the visual information available to the bee during the flight and that these components depend on the visual appearance of objects surrounding the goal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how the visual appearance of the environment shapes the bees’ behavior and how the bees’ behavior, in turn, shapes the visual information available to the bees.
the question how the bees’ behavior can be shaped to optimize the processing of visual input.
the analysis of the visual information processing during the localization of visual landmarks and its relation to behavioral strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prototypical movements are a function of the bees’ distance to the landmarks and the visual appearance of the landmarks.
bees adaptively change their flight behavior in order to gain information from the visual environment.
the prototypical movements are not fixed, but rather depend on the visual information that is available at a given time and the bees’ current position and orientation relative to it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
bees adapt their flight behavior to the visual cues that they see.
the bees’ flight behavior is adapted to the nature of available visual cues.
bees can use the visual appearance of objects to adapt their behavior to facilitate information processing during homing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the visual appearance of objects surrounding a goal influences the prototypical components of honeybee homing flight behavior.
the bees’ behavior during goal localization is highly adaptive and depends on the visual appearance of landmarks.
bees use different behavioral strategies when navigating towards a goal surrounded by landmarks of different appearance.
